Diodore of Tarsus
dī´ō-dōr ŏv tär´sŭs
n. (Diodore of Tarsus, d. c. 390, bishop of Tarsus and founder of the Antiochene school of interpretation, teacher of John Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia)
Greek Diodoros, gift of Zeus; Tarsus in Cilicia, the city of the apostle Paul.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Diodore of Tarsus led the ascetic school at Antioch that trained the two greatest preachers and expositors of the next generation, and he set its principle: the interpreter must give the sense the words bear, in their history and order, and must not substitute a spiritual meaning for the plain one. He wrote a treatise whose title states the programme — on the difference between theoria and allegory — granting that a text may have a contemplative depth while denying that it may be made to mean what it does not say. This is the discipline of Neh 8:8, where the Levites “read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading,” and of Philip's question in Act 8:30, “Understandest thou what thou readest?” The honour is real: expository preaching as the church has known it at its best descends from Antioch and not from Alexandria. The defect is equally real and was inherited by his pupils — a reluctance to see Christ in the Old Testament where the New Testament plainly finds Him, and a Christology that kept the natures so distinct that the Person came apart.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to expound as to explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.

expand to see more

EXPOUND', v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret; as, to expound a text of scripture.

2. To lay open; to examine.

LIT'ERAL, a. According to the letter; primitive; real; not figurative or metaphorical.

Key Scripture

Neh 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

Act 8:30 — "And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?"

Luk 24:45 — "Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,"

2Pe 3:16 — "As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction."

Modern Corruption

Antioch was right about the letter and short on the Lord, and Alexandria was right about the Lord and reckless with the letter; the church needed both corrections and took neither cleanly.

expand to see more

The Antiochene instinct is the one this dictionary follows: the words mean what they say, and the expositor's first duty is to give the sense. Against the Alexandrian habit of finding the Trinity in a number and the soul's ascent in a place-name, Diodore was simply correct, and 2Pe 3:16 warns what becomes of those who “wrest” the Scriptures. But a method that will not receive the New Testament's own readings of the Old has stopped being literal and become selective, since the plainest fact about Psa 22 is the use the Gospels make of it.

The deeper failure was Christological and followed from the same temper. Holding the two natures firmly apart protected the true humanity and lost the unity of the Person, and from Diodore through Theodore to Nestorius the line runs straight. Chalcedon gave the settlement both schools needed: one Person in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation. The recovery is to take Antioch's discipline with Chalcedon's confession, reading the text as it stands and confessing the Christ the whole canon declares — for it was the risen Lord who “opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Luk 24:45).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew parash (H6567), to make distinct; Greek anaginosko (G314), to read; strebloo (G4761), to wrest or twist.

Hebrew parash (H6567) — to separate, to make distinct; Nehemiah 8:8.

Hebrew sekel (H7922) — sense, understanding; Nehemiah 8:8.

Greek anaginosko (G314) — to read, to know again; Acts 8:30.

Greek dianoigo (G1272) — to open thoroughly; Luke 24:45.

Greek strebloo (G4761) — to twist, to wrest; 2 Peter 3:16.

Usage

"“read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense” (Neh 8:8) — the Antiochene charter."

"“Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30) — the expositor's question."

"“which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest” (2Pe 3:16) — the abuse he opposed."
